Chronic Pain

LO 1–6 Nociplastic pain Leading cause of US disability
How boards would word it

"A 52-year-old woman presents with widespread body pain and fatigue that has persisted for the past 8 months. She reports the pain is difficult to localize, affecting her neck, shoulders, back, and legs diffusely rather than one specific joint or muscle. She has no history of trauma, and prior workup including inflammatory markers, imaging, and nerve conduction studies has been unremarkable. She describes tenderness to light touch throughout the affected areas and reports that her sleep is significantly disrupted, alongside difficulty concentrating and low mood. Which of the following best describes the underlying pain classification?"

Answer: Nociplastic pain
What to look for: duration >3 months, regional/diffuse (not discrete) distribution, no identifiable structural or inflammatory cause despite a full workup, evoked hypersensitivity (allodynia), and the classic comorbidity cluster (sleep disturbance, fatigue, cognitive complaints, mood symptoms) — that combination signals nociplastic pain, not a nociceptive or neuropathic process.
1 Natural History
Definition & Epidemiology

Pain is a distressing sensory and emotional experience linked to, or resembling that linked to, current or potential tissue injury. Acute pain is proportional to injury and remits as the injury heals; chronic pain persists beyond that expected healing window and is, by definition, a disease state of its own — it can exist without any ongoing peripheral generator, driven instead by plastic changes in the central and/or peripheral nervous system.

  • Most prevalent disease worldwide; leading cause of disability in the USA
  • Prevalence estimated 11–40%; ~49% of people report pain lasting >3 months
  • ~70 million Americans report chronic pain; many are disabled by it
  • Estimated annual US cost (chronic pain + opioid use disorder): ~$560–635 billion
  • Incidence rises with age
Classification — by duration
  • Acute (<1 month) — a protective warning signal for actual/potential tissue damage; typically trauma, surgery, or acute illness
  • Subacute (1–3 months)
  • Chronic (>3 months) — no protective role; a disease entity in its own right
Classification — by type
  • Nociceptive — triggered by noxious chemical/mechanical/thermal stimuli. Somatic (Aδ fibers): localized, sharp, musculoskeletal. Visceral (C fibers): dull, diffuse, deep.
  • Neuropathic — damage/dysfunction of somatosensory or autonomic structures. Central (CNS dysfunction — e.g. poststroke pain, phantom limb pain). Peripheral (peripheral nerve damage — e.g. diabetic neuropathy, postherpetic neuralgia). Sympathetically mediated (autonomic nerve damage — e.g. complex regional pain syndrome).
  • Nociplastic — altered nociception with no clear evidence of underlying tissue damage
Pathogenesis — normal pain pathway
Nociceptors detect a noxious chemical/mechanical/thermal stimulus
→
Converted to an action potential
→
Aδ & C fibers carry afferent input to the dorsal horn
→
Spinothalamic tract → thalamus
→
Pain perception + efferent modulation/reaction
Pathogenesis — how it becomes chronic
Peripheral injury (or none)
→
Nociceptor sensitization
→
Dorsal horn / CNS plasticity — axon sprouting, loss of inhibitory interneurons
→
Central sensitization
→
Nociplastic amplification ± strong emotional/psychosomatic component
→
Chronic pain state, independent of ongoing peripheral drive

Prognosis if unaddressed: these plastic changes tend to self-perpetuate rather than resolve the way an acute injury would — the longer central sensitization runs, the harder it is to reverse.

Dimensions of pain — biopsychosocial model
  • Sensory-discriminative: physical attributes — quality, localization, intensity, duration
  • Affective-motivational: the emotional unpleasantness and drive to escape/avoid the stimulus
  • Cognitive-evaluative: mental interpretation shaped by attention, memory, beliefs, expectations
  • Behavioral: motor (facial expression, guarding, limping) and autonomic (tachycardia, hypertension, diaphoresis, pupillary dilation) responses

Pain arises from a dynamic interaction of biological (tissue injury, genetics), psychological (beliefs, coping, catastrophizing), and social (support system, work) factors. In chronic pain specifically, the psychological/social components often amplify and sustain the experience — frequently contributing more to distress and disability than the original injury itself.

2 Clinical Presentation
Characteristics
  • Duration usually indeterminate; persists past normal healing time (>3 months)
  • Often refractory to treatment; disrupts sleep and normal living; serves no adaptive purpose
  • Etiology: injury, malignancy, non-life-threatening conditions, or no apparent cause — may be a symptom or a diagnosis, nociceptive and/or neuropathic
  • Classified by region affected (head, chest, back, etc.) or by process (nociplastic, neuropathic, central, inflammatory, cancer pain)

Nociceptive

  • Real/threatened tissue damage
  • Somatic (Aδ): sharp, localized
  • Visceral (C): dull, diffuse, deep

Nociplastic

  • Altered central nociception
  • No clear tissue damage or somatosensory lesion

Neuropathic

  • Central: poststroke pain, phantom limb
  • Peripheral: diabetic neuropathy, PHN
  • Sympathetic: CRPS
Nociplastic pain — diagnostic criteria & comorbidities

≥3 months duration, regional (not discrete) distribution, pain not fully explained by nociceptive/neuropathic mechanisms, plus evoked hypersensitivity (static/dynamic allodynia, heat/cold allodynia, painful after-sensations) localized to the painful region.

Frequent comorbidities: sensitivity to sound/light/odor, fragmented sleep, fatigue and cognitive complaints.

Radiating pain

  • Spreads along a specific nerve's path; nerve root irritation/injury
  • Classic example: sciatica — sciatic nerve compression from degenerative disc disease, pain down the leg along the nerve

Phantom limb syndrome

  • Phantom sensation (limb feels present) vs. phantom pain (burning/tingling/shooting/electric)
  • Mechanism: somatosensory cortex reorganization after amputation
  • Diagnose only after excluding stump pathology (infection, ischemia, neuroma)
  • Tx: mirror therapy, TENS, NMDA antagonists, adjuvants (TCAs, anticonvulsants); prevent with perioperative regional anesthesia
Referred pain — classic vignette pattern-matching

Pain perceived at a site distant from its source, projected onto the dermatome/myotome sharing the same spinal segment. High-yield examples: right shoulder pain in cholecystitis; left shoulder pain with diaphragmatic irritation (splenic rupture — Kehr sign, or perforated PUD); left-sided chest/arm pain in MI; periumbilical pain in early appendicitis.

Referred pain of internal organs — visceral afferents project onto the shared dermatome, most intense at specific points within it, not the whole dermatome (click to zoom)
OrganDermatomeProjection
DiaphragmC4Shoulders
HeartT3–4Left chest
EsophagusT4–5Retrosternal
StomachT6–9Epigastrium
Liver, gallbladderT10–L1Right upper quadrant
Small bowelT10–L1Periumbilical

BladderT11–L1Suprapubic

Table vs. diagram discrepancy worth flagging: the reference table lists stomach as T6–9, while the diagram above labels it T6–T7 — the diagram is the more precise figure if a question hinges on that exact range.

3 Diagnostic Workup
CategoryFindings / Use
Neurologic & structural examSensory changes, hypersensitivity signs, structural assessment of the affected region
ElectrodiagnosticsEMG/NCS to characterize peripheral nerve involvement
CT / MRIMainly to rule out other structural or malignant causes — not to "find" chronic pain itself
Pain assessment tools
A: Numeric rating scale (0–10) · B: Visual analog scale (0–100) · C: Faces/verbal descriptor-type scale (click to zoom)
  • Numeric rating scale (NRS): most common, 0–10
  • Visual analog scale (VAS): visual equivalents, suitable for children
  • Verbal descriptor scale
  • PEG scale: validated impact scale specifically for chronic pain (pain, enjoyment, general activity)
  • Pain diary: regular documentation to identify peaks/triggers and optimize treatment
  • Nonverbal patients: use a specialized nonverbal pain scale plus caregiver-supplied history
Equity in pain assessment

Pain is subjective — scales track one patient's pain and response to treatment over time, and cannot be used to compare intensity between patients. Be aware of implicit bias: Hispanic and Black patients are less likely to receive any and/or appropriate analgesia than White patients even when reported pain scores are identical.

4 Treatment
WHO analgesic ladder

By mouth (oral preferred) · by the clock (fixed-time regular dosing, not just PRN) · by the ladder (step up if pain persists). If PRN medication is needed ≥3×/day, the regular regimen is likely inadequate — review it. Always use the minimum effective dose for the shortest duration.

Pain severityNon-opioidMild opioidStrong opioidAdjuvant
Step I — MildIncludeAvoidAvoidIf required
Step II — ModerateIncludeConsiderAvoidIf required
Step III — SevereIncludeConsiderConsiderIf required
By modality

Pharmacologic

  • Non-opioid: acetaminophen; NSAIDs (ibuprofen/naproxen first-line); celecoxib (COX-2, preferred in PUD)
  • Opioids: oxycodone, hydromorphone, tramadol, tapentadol — combine with non-opioids; avoid tramadol in epilepsy; caution in asthma/resp. depression, bowel obstruction, biliary colic, head injury
  • Combination: codeine/APAP, hydrocodone/APAP, hydrocodone/ibuprofen, oxycodone/APAP
  • Topical: lidocaine patch (postherpetic neuralgia); diclofenac patch/gel (osteoarthritis)
  • Adjuvants: anticonvulsants — gabapentin, pregabalin, carbamazepine (neuropathic pain); muscle relaxants — cyclobenzaprine, methocarbamol, baclofen (spasticity-related pain); antidepressants — TCAs (amitriptyline), SNRIs (duloxetine — the only FDA-approved antidepressant for chronic pain)

Interventional / Surgical

  • Nerve blocks, radiofrequency ablation, spinal cord stimulator
  • Intra-articular glucocorticoid or epidural steroid injections
  • Neuromodulation / nerve ablation techniques
  • Surgery: tissue removal or disruption of nociceptive pathways

Physical Medicine

  • PT/OT referral, structural assessment-directed care
  • Massage, thermotherapy (e.g. focused ultrasound)
  • Desensitization techniques
  • Regular exercise / exercise therapy

Psychological & Complementary

  • Relaxation training, progressive muscle relaxation, mindfulness, biofeedback
  • Cognitive behavioral therapy, hypnosis
  • Acupuncture; OMM (e.g. spinal manipulation for low back pain/tension headache); mind-body practices (yoga, tai chi)
5 Monitoring & Complications
Big picture

Track tolerance, addiction (opioid use disorder risk), deepening mood disorders, and opioid-induced hyperalgesia. Classic exam trap: many long-term complications of chronic pain trace back to treatment, not just the underlying disease.

Non-opioid agentComplicationPrevention / Management
AcetaminophenHepatotoxicity (↑ transaminases, acute liver failure)Avoid in liver failure; caution with reduced liver function
NSAIDs / COX-2 inhibitorsCardiovascular (MI, stroke, CHF)Avoid non-aspirin NSAIDs post-CABG/recent MI; caution in severe heart failure
NSAIDs / COX-2 inhibitorsGI (gastritis, PUD, bleeding)Consider PPI with long-term use; avoid with bowel perforation/surgery
NSAIDs / COX-2 inhibitorsKidney impairment (AKI, hyperkalemia)Avoid or use cautiously with impaired kidney function
NSAIDs / COX-2 inhibitorsHypersensitivity ± rare severe skin reactions (SJS/TEN)Avoid with prior NSAID/ASA hypersensitivity; stop if rash develops
Opioid complicationPrevention / Management
Respiratory depressionAvoid with severe sleep-disordered breathing/asthma; monitor for hypoxia/bradypnea; naloxone for overdose
Nausea / vomitingAntiemetic; metoclopramide preferred if gastric stasis/constipation
ConstipationStart a bowel regimen at initiation of therapy
Mental status changes (delirium, hallucinations)Reduce polypharmacy; consider haloperidol for agitated delirium
Opioid use disorder / overdoseLowest effective dose, short-acting agents, risk stratification, naloxone education

Also seen: urinary retention, myoclonus, neuroendocrine effects (hypogonadism, hypocortisolism, hyperprolactinemia), pruritus — usually managed with dose reduction or opioid rotation.

6 Prevention & Health Promotion
Modifiable strategy

Early, adequate intervention for acute pain is the main lever — treating pain aggressively and early, before central sensitization sets in, is the best-evidenced way to prevent the transition to a chronic pain state. At every step, use the minimum effective dose for the shortest duration to limit medication-driven complications, and favor multimodal (pharmacologic + nonpharmacologic) strategies to reduce opioid exposure.

Pearl

The nociceptive / nociplastic / neuropathic split (not just "organic vs. psychogenic") is the classification boards now expect. Fibromyalgia is the prototype nociplastic condition — not simply "medically unexplained pain."

Pearl

Referred-pain vignettes are classic bait: left shoulder pain isn't always cardiac or MSK — think splenic rupture (Kehr sign) or a perforated ulcer irritating the diaphragm.

Migraine Headache

LO 1–6 ♀ : ♂ ≈ 3:1 Aura in ~25% Attacks 4–72 hr
How boards would word it

"A 27-year-old woman presents with recurrent headaches occurring 2–3 times per month for the past year. She describes the pain as unilateral and throbbing, typically starting on the right side, lasting between 12 and 24 hours. She reports associated nausea and says she must lie down in a dark, quiet room during attacks because light and sound worsen the pain. About 20 minutes before the headache begins, she sometimes sees flashing zigzag lines in her vision that resolve completely before the headache starts. Physical and neurological examination is normal. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?"

Answer: Migraine with aura
What to look for: recurrent unilateral throbbing headache (4–72h) with photophobia/phonophobia and nausea, plus a fully reversible visual aura (<60 min) preceding it — that triad, alongside a normal exam, is the classic pattern. Boards often add a "must lie still" detail specifically to contrast with cluster headache's restlessness.
▶
▶ Migraine — physiology, pathology, clinical manifestations, diagnosis, treatment
Video — "Migraine - physiology, pathology, clinical manifestations, diagnosis, treatment" (YouTube)
1 Natural History
Definition & Epidemiology

A benign, recurring syndrome of headache, nausea, vomiting, and/or other neurologic-dysfunction symptoms in varying combinations.

  • ~18% of women, ~6% of men (~20% of the population overall)
  • Most common headache type in children
  • ~70% have a positive family history; prevalence higher in lower-income groups
  • Onset typically adolescence/early adulthood, peak incidence in the 30s
Etiology & Risk Factors / Triggers

Exact etiology unclear; genetic predisposition produces a cortex that habituates poorly to stimuli. Recognized triggers: hormonal shifts (menstruation, OCPs), chronobiologic changes, vasodilators, certain foods/drinks (tyramine, alcohol, caffeine), fasting/dehydration, poor sleep, stress, weather changes, sensory input, trauma.

Pathogenesis — trigeminovascular pathway
Trigger (hormonal / dietary / stress / sleep)
→
Cortical spreading depression in a hyperexcitable cortex
→
Activation of trigeminal (CN V) afferents on meningeal vessels
→
Release of CGRP / substance P
→
Neurogenic inflammation + meningeal vasodilation
→
Activation & sensitization of meningeal nociceptors
→
Pain + associated autonomic/GI symptoms

Vasodilation is now considered a downstream epiphenomenon rather than the primary driver of the headache.

Evolution if unmanaged: migraine → tension-type features → mixed headache → chronic daily headache (≥15 headache days/month for >3 months) — often accelerated by medication overuse.

2 Clinical Presentation
The four phases

Prodrome (24–48h before; yawning, mood/appetite changes) → Aura (~25% of attacks; fully reversible focal neuro symptoms lasting <60 min — scintillating scotoma, other visual/sensory/speech symptoms, no motor symptoms) → Headache (unilateral in ~60%, throbbing/pounding, 4–72h, worsened by activity, with photophobia/phonophobia/nausea/vomiting) → Postdrome (exhaustion, muscle weakness, appetite change).

  • Throbbing character in ~85%; photophobia ~90%; nausea ~80%
  • Cutaneous allodynia may occur — light touch of skin triggers pain
  • Autonomic head symptoms are common

Hemiplegic migraine

  • Motor weakness + typical aura, ~72h
  • Familial or sporadic
  • Key differential: epilepsy

Vestibular migraine

  • Most common cause of spontaneous episodic vertigo
  • ≥5 vestibular episodes, ≤72h each

Migraine with brainstem aura

  • ≥2 reversible brainstem symptoms (dysarthria, vertigo, diplopia, ataxia)
  • No motor or retinal symptoms
Differentiating migraine vs. tension-type vs. cluster headache

Migraine: unilateral, throbbing/hammering, 4–72h, nausea/vomiting + photophobia/phonophobia, exercise worsens it. Tension-type: bilateral, dull band-like pressure, no nausea/vomiting, exertion does not worsen it. Cluster: unilateral periorbital piercing/burning pain with ipsilateral autonomic signs (lacrimation, rhinorrhea), short attacks (30–40 min) that cluster over weeks, male-predominant, often nocturnal.

Migraine fact sheet — triggers, character of pain, additional symptoms, prophylaxis (click to zoom)
Migraine vs. tension-type vs. cluster headache — character, course, symptoms (click to zoom)

Red flags that push toward neuroimaging: first/worst headache, onset after age 50, "crash" (sudden, severe) onset, unusual/prolonged/persistent aura, a new change from the patient's baseline pattern, status migrainosus, or posttraumatic migraine.

See the Tension-Type Headache panel for that condition's full LO 1–6 breakdown.

3 Diagnostic Workup
CategoryFindings / Use
History & PERecurrent attacks meeting criteria (≥5 attacks without aura, or ≥2 with aura) — unilateral + pulsating + moderate/severe + worsened by routine activity, plus nausea/vomiting or photophobia/phonophobia
Red-flag screenDrives the imaging decision — migraine itself needs none
NeuroimagingMRI preferred over CT; reserved for red flags or atypical features, not routine migraine
LabsNot routinely indicated; consider urine hCG in reproductive-age patients to guide drug choice
4 Treatment
By phase

Acute / Abortive

  • General measures: dark/quiet room, hydration
  • First-line: NSAIDs/acetaminophen ± caffeine
  • Antiemetics (metoclopramide, prochlorperazine) if nausea present
  • Triptans (most effective at attack onset) or ergotamines — never combine the two classes
  • CGRP antagonists (ubrogepant, rimegepant) / lasmiditan as alternatives
  • Avoid opioids as first-line — unclear efficacy, can worsen nausea

Prophylactic

  • Indicated for frequent/disabling attacks or when abortive therapy fails/is contraindicated
  • Beta-blockers (propranolol)
  • Anticonvulsants (topiramate, divalproex)
  • TCAs (amitriptyline)
  • CGRP monoclonal antibodies / gepants, OnabotulinumtoxinA (chronic migraine)
  • Candesartan (off-label)

Nonpharmacologic

  • Regular sleep, meals, exercise
  • Trigger identification & avoidance
  • Biofeedback, relaxation training
  • Some evidence for acupuncture
5 Monitoring & Complications
What to track
  • Status migrainosus: attack ≥72h, exceptionally severe, often medication-overuse related — treated with stepwise escalation (IV fluids, antiemetic, NSAID, dihydroergotamine, dexamethasone, ± valproate), with inpatient care if refractory
  • Medication overuse headache: triptans >9 days/month or analgesics >14 days/month risk perpetuating daily headache — a headache diary helps catch this early
  • Track progression toward chronic migraine (≥15 headache days/month for >3 months)
6 Prevention & Health Promotion
Protective factors
  • Regular sleep, regular meals, regular exercise
  • Biofeedback, healthy lifestyle overall, trigger avoidance

Pharmacologic prophylaxis is reserved for frequent/disabling attacks. Key safety point: migraine with aura is an absolute contraindication to estrogen-containing contraceptives (increased ischemic stroke risk).

Pearl

SUMoTRIPtANs = SUMaTRIPtANs, used for both migraine and cluster headache. POUND (Pulsatile, One-day duration, Unilateral, Nausea, Disabling) is the fast bedside screen for migraine without aura.

Tension-Type Headache

LO 1–6 Most common headache overall 30 min–7 days
How boards would word it

"A 34-year-old man presents with a headache that has been occurring almost daily for the past two weeks, coinciding with a stressful work deadline. He describes the pain as a constant, dull pressure that feels like a tight band around his entire head. The pain is present on both sides and does not worsen with physical activity or exertion. He denies nausea, vomiting, and sensitivity to light, though he notes mild sensitivity to loud noise. Neurological examination is normal, though palpation of the pericranial muscles reveals mild tenderness. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?"

Answer: Tension-type headache
What to look for: bilateral, dull/band-like pressure that is not worsened by exertion, with no more than one autonomic symptom (here: mild phonophobia only, no photophobia or nausea). That specific absence of migraine features, paired with bilateral banding pain, is the tell.
▶
▶ Tension Headache USMLE Mnemonic
Video — "Tension Headache USMLE Mnemonic" (YouTube)
1 Natural History
Definition & Epidemiology

Defined strictly by its signs and symptoms: dull, non-pulsating, bilateral head pain of mild-to-moderate severity (synonyms: tension headache, muscle tension headache).

  • Most common headache type in adults; ~86% of people have at least one lifetime episode (lifetime prevalence estimates range 30–90%)
  • ♀ > ♂ — roughly 5:4 for episodic TTH, widening to ~3:1 for chronic daily headache
  • Peak incidence in the 30s–40s
Etiology

Exact pathophysiology unknown — despite the name, it is not directly caused by muscle tension. Thought to involve sensitization of primary afferent fibers and/or central trigeminal pathways. Exacerbating factors: fatigue, poor sleep, poor posture, anxiety, stress, depression.

Pathogenesis (poorly clarified)
Trigger — stress, fatigue, poor posture, mood disturbance
→
Sensitization of pericranial myofascial afferents ± central trigeminal pathways
→
Lowered pain threshold in head/neck muscles
→
Bilateral, band-like pressing pain

Unlike migraine, there is no established vascular/trigeminovascular inflammatory cascade here — the mechanism is comparatively under-characterized, which is itself a testable point.

2 Clinical Presentation
Episodic TTH
  • Lasts 30 minutes to 7 days
  • Pressing, nonpulsating, "vise-like" quality; mild-to-moderate; bilateral (holocranial/bifrontal)
  • Not aggravated by physical activity
  • No nausea/vomiting; at most one autonomic symptom (photophobia or phonophobia, not both)
  • Palpation may reveal pericranial muscle tenderness; neurological exam is normal
Tension headache fact sheet — epidemiology, character of pain, triggers, additional symptoms, prophylaxis (click to zoom)
ICHD categoryFrequencyDurationAutonomic symptoms
Infrequent episodic≥10 episodes, <1 day/month (<12 days/yr)30 min–7 daysNo N/V; ≤1 of photophobia/phonophobia
Frequent episodic≥10 episodes on 1–14 days/month, >3 months (12–179 days/yr)30 min–7 daysOnly one of photophobia, phonophobia, or mild nausea
Chronic≥15 days/month, >3 months (≥180 days/yr)Hours–days, may be continuousNo moderate/severe nausea or vomiting
Chronic daily headache

≥15 headache days/month for >3 months (≥180 days/year); same pain characteristics as episodic TTH. Can be associated with analgesic overuse, or represent a transformed migraine.

Risk factors for progressing to chronic daily headache: obesity, history of frequent headaches, caffeine consumption, overuse of acute headache medication, sleep disturbances, mood disorders (anxiety, depression).

Differentiating tension vs. migraine vs. cluster headache
Pain localization — tension (bifrontal/holocranial), migraine (unilateral periorbital/temporal), cluster (unilateral periorbital with red eye/tearing) (click to zoom)

Tension: holocranial/bifrontal, dull, no autonomic symptoms. Migraine: unilateral, with autonomic symptoms (nausea/vomiting, photophobia, phonophobia). Cluster: unilateral, periorbital, with conjunctival injection, lacrimation, rhinorrhea, nasal congestion, Horner syndrome, and facial/forehead sweating.

Red flags prompting workup beyond a clinical TTH diagnosis: thunderclap onset, fever/systemic symptoms, focal neuro deficits, onset >50 years, a pattern change or new-onset headache, positional headache, signs of ↑ICP (papilledema), or posttraumatic onset.

3 Diagnostic Workup
Diagnostic criteria

At least two of: dull/pressing/nonpulsating quality · mild-to-moderate intensity · bilateral · no increase with exertion — plus not better explained by another headache disorder. Primarily a clinical diagnosis.

CategoryFindings / Use
Neurologic examExpected to be normal
Pericranial palpationMay reveal increased muscle tenderness
Headache/symptom diaryHelps confirm diagnosis and guide management if recurrent
Red-flag screenRules out secondary causes and curable conditions before settling on TTH; screen for comorbid depression/anxiety
4 Treatment
By type / modality

Episodic — Pharmacologic

  • NSAIDs (ibuprofen, naproxen, diclofenac), aspirin, or acetaminophen
  • Counsel against use >15 days/month (medication overuse headache risk)
  • Opioids are not recommended — increase medication overuse headache risk without added benefit

Chronic / Frequent — Prophylactic

  • Amitriptyline is first-line
  • Alternatives: beta-blockers, divalproex sodium, other TCAs, tizanidine (methysergide historically used, largely supplanted)
  • Chronic daily headache: taper off the offending overused analgesic; a short tapering course of prednisone or long-acting NSAIDs can bridge withdrawal

Nonpharmacologic

  • Lifestyle/behavioral modification: stress reduction, sleep hygiene, exercise, weight reduction
  • CBT, relaxation training, biofeedback
  • Physical therapy, manipulation (OMM), acupuncture, yoga
  • In children, nonpharmacologic measures are preferred over prophylactic medication
5 Monitoring & Complications
What to track
  • Medication overuse headache: the central risk with prolonged (>15 days/month) NSAID/analgesic use, and the reason opioids are avoided
  • Drug addiction and rebound effects with chronic analgesic use
  • Watch for evolution into chronic daily headache, including the possibility that it represents a transformed migraine
6 Prevention & Health Promotion
Modifiable strategy

Prophylactic therapy (amitriptyline first-line) for chronic or frequent episodic TTH. Beyond medication, address the modifiable risk factors for progression to chronic daily headache directly: weight, caffeine intake, sleep quality, mood disorders, and medication overuse itself.

Pearl

TTH is the "boring" headache boards want you to reach by exclusion of migraine/cluster features — bilateral + no worsening with activity + no more than one autonomic symptom. But don't stop there: a chronic, daily version of that same headache can represent a transformed migraine, so pair chronicity with the patient's prior headache history before closing the diagnosis.

Cluster Headache

LO 1–6 ♂ > ♀ 15 min–3 hr attacks
How boards would word it

"A 34-year-old man presents to the emergency department with severe pain around his right eye that began 30 minutes ago and has progressively worsened. He describes the pain as sharp and burning, rating it 10/10. He appears agitated, pacing around the room and unable to sit still. On examination, his right eye is red and tearing, with mild eyelid swelling and a constricted pupil compared to the left. He reports that this is the fourth similar episode this week, each lasting under an hour, and that they tend to occur at night. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?"

Answer: Cluster headache
What to look for: unilateral periorbital pain with a short duration (<3h) and a cyclical/nightly pattern, ipsilateral autonomic signs (conjunctival injection, lacrimation, partial Horner's — ptosis + miosis), and restlessness/agitation rather than a preference to lie still. That behavioral clue plus the autonomic signs is what separates it from migraine.
▶
▶ Cluster Headaches — symptoms, pathophysiology, treatment
Video — "Cluster Headaches - symptoms, pathophysiology, treatment" (YouTube)
1 Natural History
Definition & Epidemiology

An episodic, explosive, severe unilateral headache centered in the periorbital area (less commonly temporal). Synonyms: migrainous neuralgia, histamine cephalalgia (Horton's headache), sphenopalatine neuralgia.

  • Rare — ~0.1% of the population (~1 per 1000)
  • ♂ > ♀; sources vary between 3:1 and 5:1
  • Peak incidence 20–40 years (third–fourth decade)
  • ~90% episodic pattern, ~10% chronic
Etiology

Not entirely understood; a weak genetic component is suspected. Risk factor: tobacco use. Triggers: alcohol, histamine, seasonal fluctuations, nitroglycerine, volatile substances (solvents, oil-based paint), insomnia, bright lights.

Pathogenesis
Trigger (alcohol, volatile substances, circadian/seasonal factors)
→
Activation of the trigeminovascular system
→
Activation of the (parasympathetic) sphenopalatine ganglion
→
Ipsilateral pain + cranial autonomic symptom complex

Temporal pattern: cluster periods/bouts typically 1–2×/year (can be seasonal), each with remission of 6 months to 2 years between bouts. Considered chronic if remission between bouts is <3 months. Attacks tend to strike at a consistent time of day for a given patient and often occur at night.

2 Clinical Presentation
Attack characteristics
  • Rapid onset, over minutes (~5–15 min)
  • Duration 15 minutes to 3 hours (most commonly ~30–45 min); typically 1–3 attacks/24h
  • Agonizing, strictly unilateral, periorbital and/or temporal (± infraorbital); can radiate to forehead, temple, cheek, rarely ear/occiput/neck
  • Quality: constant boring pressure, burning, stabbing
  • Ipsilateral autonomic symptoms: conjunctival injection, lacrimation, rhinorrhea/nasal congestion, eye erythema, and partial Horner syndrome (ptosis + miosis, no anhidrosis)
  • Restlessness/agitation, pacing — unlike migraine patients, who prefer to lie motionless in a dark, quiet room
Cluster headache fact sheet — epidemiology, triggers, character of pain, autonomic signs, course of an attack (click to zoom)
Differentiating from migraine & tension-type headache

Cluster is unilateral and periorbital like migraine, but far shorter (minutes–hours vs. 4–72h), with prominent ipsilateral autonomic signs (migraine's autonomic symptoms are systemic — nausea/photophobia/phonophobia — not focal to one eye), male-predominant, and defined by restlessness rather than a preference to lie still. See the Migraine and Tension-Type Headache panels for their full comparisons.

3 Diagnostic Workup
CategoryFindings / Use
HistoryPrimary basis for diagnosis — exact description and timing of attacks (cyclical pattern, duration, ipsilateral autonomic signs)
Neurologic examPhysical findings otherwise unremarkable between attacks
MRIReserved for patients with red flags for headache, to rule out a secondary cause
4 Treatment
By phase

Acute

  • First-line: 100% oxygen (FiO2 100%, first choice if available); triptans — subcutaneous sumatriptan or intranasal zolmitriptan (apply nasal spray in the nostril unaffected by congestion for better absorption)
  • Other options: IV dihydroergotamine, topical lidocaine, butorphanol, intranasal capsaicin
  • Avoid standard analgesics (acetaminophen, NSAIDs, opioids) — ineffective here and risk medication overuse headache with frequent use

Prophylactic

  • Verapamil is first-line
  • If ineffective/not tolerated: lithium, melatonin, topiramate, baclofen, divalproex sodium (methysergide historically used)
  • Emerging: galcanezumab, civamide
5 Monitoring & Complications
What to track
  • Track whether the pattern remains episodic (~90%) or becomes chronic (~10%, remission <3 months between bouts)
  • Resistance to all pharmacologic therapy — consider percutaneous radiofrequency retrogasserian rhizotomy in refractory cases
  • Avoid standard analgesics long-term given medication overuse headache risk without analgesic benefit
6 Prevention & Health Promotion
Modifiable strategy

Trigger avoidance (alcohol, volatile solvents/oil-based paint, bright lights, poor sleep) and smoking cessation (tobacco is a risk factor). Starting prophylactic therapy proactively during a known cluster period reduces attack burden.

Pearl

Restless and pacing, not lying still — that behavioral tell separates cluster from migraine at the bedside before you even reach the autonomic signs. And "partial" Horner syndrome here specifically means ptosis + miosis without anhidrosis.

Seizures & Epilepsy

LO 1–6 Prevalence ~5–10/1000 Epilepsy ≠ seizure
How boards would word it

"A 24-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after an episode in which he suddenly lost consciousness, fell to the ground, and exhibited rhythmic jerking of all four extremities lasting about 2 minutes. His roommate reports that he bit his tongue and was incontinent of urine during the event. Afterward, he was confused and drowsy for approximately 20 minutes before returning to baseline. This is his second such episode in the past 8 months; the first occurred without any identifiable trigger. Which of the following statements is most accurate regarding this patient's condition?"

Answer: This meets criteria for epilepsy (≥2 unprovoked seizures >24 hours apart)
What to look for: the seizure semiology (LOC, tongue biting, incontinence, postictal confusion) just tells you it was a generalized tonic-clonic seizure — the diagnosis of epilepsy hinges on a separate detail: the recurrence count and the fact that it was unprovoked. Don't let the dramatic seizure description distract from that.
▶
▶ Seizures and epilepsy
Video — "Seizures and epilepsy" (YouTube)
1 Natural History
Definitions

A seizure is a paroxysmal event of excessive, hypersynchronous, uncontrolled neuronal activity — an involuntary change in behavior from synchronous neuron firing, which can arise from structural, metabolic, or drug-induced causes. Epilepsy is the chronic disorder of recurrent, unprovoked seizures — not a synonym for seizure. All people with epilepsy have had seizures; not all people with seizures have epilepsy.

Epilepsy is diagnosed when a patient has any one of: (1) ≥2 unprovoked or reflex seizures >24h apart, (2) one unprovoked/reflex seizure plus high recurrence risk (e.g., after TBI, stroke, CNS infection), or (3) diagnosis of an epilepsy syndrome.

  • Provoked (acute symptomatic) seizure: occurs at/soon after an acute systemic or CNS insult (stroke, TBI, CNS infection, metabolic disturbance, drug/alcohol intoxication or withdrawal)
  • Unprovoked seizure: no identifiable cause, or beyond the acute window after a CNS insult
  • Reflex seizure: consistently evoked by a specific trigger (e.g., flashing lights)
  • Ictal / interictal / postictal: during / between / after a seizure
  • Drug-resistant epilepsy: ≥2 AEDs (sequential or combined) have failed
  • Syncope is not a seizure — it's loss of consciousness from reduced cerebral blood flow
Epidemiology
  • Incidence of unprovoked seizures: ~61/100,000 (~1.2/1,000 including all seizure types)
  • Incidence of epilepsy: ~79/100,000; recurrent-seizure incidence ~0.5/1,000
  • Prevalence of epilepsy: ~8.5/1,000 (Pillard cites a broader 5–10/1,000 range)
Etiology

Fewer than half of patients with seizures have an identifiable cause. Categories: genetic (ion channel/receptor mutations, chromosomal syndromes, inborn metabolic errors, mitochondrial disease), structural (perinatal injury, tumors*, TBI, hippocampal sclerosis, congenital malformations), metabolic, immune (autoimmune encephalitis), infectious (acute or chronic CNS infection*). (* = higher-yield "serious" causes per course notes)

Age groupCommon causes
Neonates/infants (<6mo)Genetic, congenital malformation, perinatal injury/infection, metabolic (hypoglycemia, hypocalcemia, PKU); West syndrome (1–6mo)
Older infants/children (<10y)Febrile seizures, genetic (Rolandic epilepsy), infection, TBI, congenital malformation, metabolic disorders
Adolescents (10–18y)TBI, encephalitis, genetic disorders, illicit substance use
Adults (18–60y)Alcohol withdrawal, TBI, illicit substances, brain tumors, infection, metabolic disorders
Older adults (>60y)Cerebrovascular disease, TBI, brain tumors, abscesses, neurodegenerative disease

Triggers (in patients with or without epilepsy): fever, sleep deprivation, flashing lights, alcohol, excessive exertion, stress/strong emotions, loud music, hormonal/menstrual changes.

Pathogenesis
Predisposing insult (structural / metabolic / genetic / toxic / withdrawal)
→
Lowered seizure threshold, neuronal hyperexcitability
→
Excessive, hypersynchronous cortical neuron firing
→
Focal or generalized spread across cortical networks
→
Transient neurologic symptoms ± postictal state
Neurons form electrical networks (like roads/traffic lights) — a seizure is uncontrolled firing within that network; the more neurons involved, the more widespread the seizure (click to zoom)
2 Clinical Presentation
ILAE 2017 classification

Focal (originates in one hemisphere) — aware or impaired awareness. Generalized (both hemispheres from onset) — always with impaired/lost consciousness. Unknown onset. Focal-to-bilateral tonic-clonic: starts focal, progresses to a bilateral convulsive phase — if it evolves quickly, the focal onset may go unnoticed and get mislabeled as primary generalized.

EEG correlate — normal background vs. a focal (partial) discharge vs. bilateral generalized discharge (click to zoom)

Focal seizure

  • Aura common (anxiety, fear, déjà vu)
  • Motor: automatisms, Jacksonian march, hyperkinetic movements
  • Nonmotor: autonomic, cognitive, emotional, sensory (visual/auditory/olfactory/gustatory)
  • Postictal Todd paralysis possible

Generalized tonic-clonic

  • Sudden LOC, no warning
  • Tonic: apnea, tongue biting, ictal cry → clonic: rhythmic jerking
  • Usually 1–3 min; postictal confusion/amnesia/fatigue

Absence (petit mal)

  • Blank stare, <10 sec, abrupt on/off
  • Subtle automatisms (lip-smacking, eye flutter)
  • No postictal confusion; triggered by hyperventilation/flashing lights
ConditionKey cluesDuration
Focal-onset seizureAura common, symptoms depend on focus, Jacksonian march, postictal paralysisUsually <2 min
Generalized motor seizureAura uncommon, LOC, tongue biting, incontinence, postictal confusionUsually <5 min
Febrile seizureAge 6mo–5y, high fever, usually generalized tonic-clonicSimple <15 min; complex ≥15 min/focal
Psychogenic nonepileptic seizure (PNES)Eyes closed & resist opening, tongue biting/incontinence rare, awareness usually intact, patient recalls event, occurs with witnesses presentTypically >5 min
Panic attackPalpitations, chest pain, dyspnea, fear of losing control — no LOCSeconds to hours
SyncopeProdromal dizziness/pallor/sweating, brief LOC, minimal postevent symptoms1–2 min
Stroke / TIANegative symptoms (weakness, vision loss), consciousness preservedMinutes–hours (TIA) to permanent (stroke)
Migraine auraPositive then negative visual symptoms, gradual onset, consciousness preserved, followed by headache≤1 hour
Breath-holding spellAge 6mo–6y, triggered by strong emotion/injury, cyanosis/pallor, brief cry then apnea≤1 min cessation of breathing
High-yield rule

Consciousness is lost only when both cerebral hemispheres or the brainstem are compromised — a seizure confined to one hemisphere should not, by itself, cause loss of consciousness in the patient.

3 Diagnostic Workup
CategoryFindings / Use
HistoryEvent description (patient if aware, witness if impaired), triggers, prodrome/aura, ictal & postictal symptoms, prior epilepsy/AED adherence, underlying conditions
Physical examInspect for fall injuries, tongue bites, skin findings (phakomatoses); cardiovascular exam
EEGIndicated for first seizure, unclear classification, or refractory seizures. Ictal: epileptiform discharges (spikes, sharp waves, spike-wave; hypsarrhythmia in West syndrome, 3Hz spike-wave in absence). Interictal is often normal — a normal EEG does NOT rule out epilepsy
MRIPreferred imaging for first-time focal seizures, to identify structural abnormalities
CTIf MRI unavailable; less sensitive for soft-tissue lesions
ECGRule out a cardiogenic cause of loss of consciousness
LabsGlucose, calcium, sodium/electrolytes, BUN; expanded workup as indicated: CBC, prolactin, toxicology, AED levels, renal/liver function
Lumbar punctureCSF analysis if CNS infection is suspected

In adults, an isolated unprovoked focal (or focal-to-bilateral tonic-clonic) seizure typically points to a structural or metabolic cause and warrants further evaluation.

4 Treatment
Acute seizure / status epilepticus (phase-based)
Phase (time from onset)Management
Early (0–5 min)Often self-limited; pharmacotherapy usually not needed. Stabilize: remove hazards, ABCDE, O2, recovery position, check glucose
Early status epilepticus (5–20 min)IV benzodiazepine (lorazepam or diazepam), first-line; IM/intranasal/buccal midazolam or rectal diazepam if no IV access; repeat q5–10min
Persistent (20–40 min)Second-line: IV fosphenytoin, valproic acid, levetiracetam, or phenobarbital
Refractory (40–60 min)Repeat second-line, or induce coma (propofol, thiopental, midazolam, pentobarbital)

Treat rapidly reversible causes concurrently: IV dextrose for hypoglycemia (± thiamine if alcohol use/malnutrition), hypertonic saline for hyponatremia, IV calcium/magnesium repletion, benzodiazepine + thiamine for alcohol withdrawal, magnesium sulfate for eclampsia.

Long-term antiepileptic drugs (AEDs)
Seizure typeFirst-line
FocalLamotrigine, levetiracetam
Generalized tonic-clonicLamotrigine, valproate
Typical absenceEthosuximide

Broader AED list from course notes: carbamazepine, phenytoin, gabapentin, oxcarbazepine, primidone, clonazepam, felbamate, topiramate, zonisamide, phenobarbital — selected by seizure type, age, and comorbidities. Monotherapy is preferred (~2/3 become seizure-free); combination therapy only if monotherapy fails, using drugs from different mechanistic classes.

Nonpharmacologic (drug-resistant epilepsy)

  • Resection (temporal lobectomy/amygdalohippocampectomy for hippocampal sclerosis; hemispherectomy for severe unilateral disease)
  • Disconnection: callosotomy, hemispherotomy
  • Vagus nerve stimulation, deep brain stimulation
  • Ketogenic diet
5 Monitoring & Complications
Acute
  • Physical trauma: tongue biting, posterior shoulder dislocation from a fall, polytrauma
  • Hyperthermia, cardiorespiratory deficits, excitotoxicity → irreversible CNS damage (e.g., cortical laminar necrosis)
  • Postictal lactic acidosis (transient, resolves in 60–90 min)
  • Status epilepticus itself: risk of cerebral edema, hyperthermia, rhabdomyolysis, cardiovascular failure
Long-term
  • Psychiatric: anxiety, depression (& suicide risk), cognitive impairment, psychosis; sleep disturbance
  • Bone disease (osteomalacia/osteoporosis) from AEDs
  • Abnormal/"interictal" personality traits, short-term memory loss
  • SUDEP (sudden unexpected death in epilepsy) — more common with intractable epilepsy, frequent (especially tonic-clonic) seizures, early onset; usually occurs during sleep
Prognosis

Recurrence after a first unprovoked seizure: ~40–50% within 2 years if no underlying brain insult (higher, ~65% over 10 years, if there was one). 60–70% of treated patients are seizure-free at 10 years. All-cause mortality is 1.6–3× the general population.

6 Prevention & Health Promotion
General

Trigger avoidance (sleep hygiene, alcohol moderation, seizure-safety precautions), strict medication adherence, and awareness of state-specific driving/legal regulations for people with epilepsy.

Pregnancy

Folic acid supplementation is recommended for all individuals of reproductive age with epilepsy. Fertility is reduced (~33% lower per course notes) and there is a higher risk of birth defects/labor complications — but ~90% of pregnant women with epilepsy still have an uneventful delivery and a healthy child. Avoid unplanned pregnancy; measure AED levels before conception and regularly throughout pregnancy. Prefer low-teratogenic-risk AEDs (lamotrigine, levetiracetam) over high-risk ones (valproate — highest risk, phenobarbital, topiramate, phenytoin) when possible.

Pearl

Epilepsy ≠ seizure: epilepsy is the disease of recurrent unprovoked seizures; a seizure is the individual event. Pair that with the differential table above — eyes that resist opening plus a normal ictal EEG points to PNES; brief prodromal dizziness/pallor points to syncope; positive-then-negative visual symptoms followed by headache point to migraine aura.

Febrile Seizures

LO 1, 2, 4 Peak age 2 yr 2–5% of children
How boards would word it

"A 20-month-old girl is brought to the emergency department after having a seizure at home. Her parents report that she had a fever of 39.4°C (103°F) due to an upper respiratory infection, and about an hour after the fever started, she had a single episode of generalized shaking of her arms and legs lasting approximately 3 minutes. She returned to her normal alert self within 15 minutes afterward. She has no history of prior seizures, and there are no focal neurological findings on examination. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?"

Answer: Reassurance and supportive care (treat the fever) — no further workup needed
What to look for: age 6mo–5y, a clear fever source, generalized (no focal features), <15 minutes, a single episode, and a quick return to baseline. That whole bundle defines a simple febrile seizure, which needs no LP, imaging, or EEG — just addressing the fever and reassuring the caregivers.

Per the source material's LO range, this panel covers Natural History, Clinical Presentation, and Treatment only — Diagnostic Workup, Monitoring & Complications, and Prevention are intentionally not built out here.

▶
▶ Febrile Seizures — Duke-NUS Medical School
Video — "Febrile Seizures - Duke-NUS Medical School" (YouTube)
1 Natural History
Definition & Classification

Seizures in children 6 months–5 years associated with fever (>38°C/100.4°F), in the absence of CNS infection, metabolic abnormality, or a history of afebrile seizures. Synonyms: febrile convulsions, fever fits.

  • Simple (~70%): generalized, <15 min, ≤1 seizure/24h
  • Complex (~20–35% depending on source): ≥15 min or >1 seizure/24h or any focal feature
  • Febrile status epilepticus (~5%): any febrile seizure >30 min, or a series totaling >30 min without full recovery between — a small fraction of febrile seizures overall, but accounts for a large share (~25–50%) of pediatric status epilepticus
Epidemiology
  • Most common pediatric seizure disorder; occurs in 2–5% of children
  • Peak incidence at 2 years of age
Etiology & Risk Factors

Exact pathophysiology unknown. Genetic predisposition (positive family history); high fever (>40°C/104°F increases risk further); viral infection (HHV-6, influenza) is the most common risk factor; recent immunization (especially MMR, DTaP); more common in winter, coinciding with peak viral season; higher incidence in children with an underlying neurologic deficit (e.g., cerebral palsy, developmental delay).

Prognosis

Not associated with increased long-term neurologic/cognitive impairment or mortality — overall prognosis is good — but there is a real recurrence risk and a small risk of later epilepsy.

  • Recurrence: ~30% if onset >12 months old; ~50% if onset <12 months. Risk factors: age <18 months at onset, seizure within 1 hour of fever onset, febrile seizures in a first-degree relative, seizure at a lower fever (<40°C). More than a third of affected children have at least one more febrile seizure.
  • Epilepsy risk: ~1% after a single simple febrile seizure; 6–8% overall after complex febrile seizures
2 Clinical Presentation
Typical course

Core temperature rises rapidly, often to ≥39°C. A generalized tonic-clonic seizure follows, lasting seconds to minutes, then a postictal fatigue period.

Tonic phase (rigid extension) followed by clonic phase (rhythmic jerking) — the same two-phase pattern as any generalized tonic-clonic seizure (click to zoom)

Simple

  • Generalized (no focal component), commonly tonic-clonic
  • <15 minutes; quick return to normal
  • Confusion/drowsiness may persist <30 min postictally

Complex

  • ≥15 min, or interrupted by abortive therapy
  • >1 seizure in 24h
  • Any focal feature
  • Postictal phase may show focal deficits or postictal (Todd) paralysis
Red flag in the presentation

Prolonged drowsiness or any new neurological abnormality after the seizure should raise concern for an underlying infectious process (e.g., meningitis) or ongoing seizure activity — not just be written off as a normal postictal state.

4 Treatment
Approach

Most simple febrile seizures resolve spontaneously within a few minutes and need no seizure-directed treatment. Search for and treat the underlying cause of fever (e.g., antibiotics for a bacterial source), and offer supportive care including antipyretics. Reassure and educate caregivers — the overall prognosis is good even though recurrence is common.

Abortive therapy

  • Indication: seizure activity lasting >5 minutes
  • Preferred IV agents: lorazepam or diazepam
  • No IV access: buccal midazolam or rectal diazepam
  • Oral diazepam has also been used

Disposition

  • Most children who return to baseline can be discharged with close pediatric follow-up
  • Consider admission for: any child who had a lumbar puncture, severe illness, recurrent seizures, neurologic abnormalities, no return to baseline, or unreliable follow-up

Prophylactic anticonvulsants are not usually indicated for simple febrile seizures. Medication choice in this age group must also account for the numerous pharmacologic contraindications common in young children.

Neonatal Seizures

LO 1–2 Birth–4 weeks Often subtle
How boards would word it

"A 3-day-old male infant, born at 39 weeks via emergency cesarean section for fetal distress, is noted by nursing staff to have episodes of rhythmic chewing movements, lip-smacking, and brief pauses in breathing. There are no observed tonic-clonic movements. The infant required resuscitation at birth for low Apgar scores. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of these episodes?"

Answer: Hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy
What to look for: the subtle, nonconvulsive presentation (chewing, lip-smacking, apnea — not a dramatic convulsion) is itself the clue that this is a neonatal seizure. Pair that recognition with the perinatal history (fetal distress, low Apgars, resuscitation), which points straight to hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy as the cause.

Per the source material's LO range (1–2), this panel covers Natural History and Clinical Presentation only. Diagnostic Workup, Treatment, Monitoring, and Prevention are intentionally not built out here, even though the source material includes substantial diagnosis/management content (EEG protocols, phenobarbital/fosphenytoin dosing, etc.) — that's deliberately out of scope for this LO range, not an oversight.

1 Natural History
Definition

The neonatal brain does not yet contain the massive numbers of myelinated axons present in the adult brain, so electrical activity cannot propagate throughout the brain the way it does in adults. As a result, neonatal seizures (occurring birth to 4 weeks of age) present with a different constellation of signs and symptoms than seizures at any older age.

Etiology

The single most common cause is hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy.

Risk factors
  • Encephalopathy following perinatal hypoxia
  • Cardiac or pulmonary conditions that risk hypoxia
  • CNS infections
  • Intracranial hemorrhage
  • Inborn errors of metabolism
  • Perinatal stroke
  • Hereditary CNS malformations
  • Birth and/or pregnancy complications; family history

See the Seizures & Epilepsy panel's age-based etiology table for how this compares to seizure causes at other ages of life.

2 Clinical Presentation
Recognition is the challenge

Clinical features are often subtle or entirely absent, which is precisely what makes neonatal seizures easy to miss.

  • Focal seizures: twitching of an individual muscle group
  • Multifocal clonic seizures: multiple muscle groups affected
  • Tonic seizures: rigid posturing of the extremities and/or trunk
  • Myoclonic seizures: brief, focal jerks
  • Subtle seizures: chewing, salivation, apnea, bicycling leg movements, other automatisms, behavioral arrest, autonomic changes
Why presentation alone isn't enough

Most seizures in neonates are subclinical, and a range of nonepileptic entities can closely mimic true neonatal seizures — which is exactly why recognition from clinical signs alone is unreliable in this age group.

Pearl

Don't wait for a classic convulsion — in a neonate, staring, chewing, apnea, or cycling leg movements can be the only visible sign of a seizure.

Status Epilepticus

LO 1–5 Medical emergency Mortality 10–50%
How boards would word it

"A 45-year-old woman with a known seizure disorder is brought to the emergency department after her husband witnessed a generalized tonic-clonic seizure. On arrival, paramedics report that she has had three seizures in a row over the past 12 minutes, without regaining consciousness between episodes. She has IV access already established. Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate treatment?"

Answer: IV lorazepam (or diazepam)
What to look for: the defining feature isn't a single seizure lasting a long time — it's repeated seizures without recovery of consciousness in between, which meets the definition of status epilepticus regardless of the older "30-minute" figure some sources cite. That recognition should immediately trigger first-line IV benzodiazepine therapy.
▶
▶ Neurology — Status Epilepticus (George Porfiris, M.D.)
Video — "Neurology – Status Epilepticus: By George Porfiris M.D." (YouTube)
1 Natural History
Definition

Convulsive seizure activity lasting longer than 30 minutes by the older/strict definition — but most current definitions use a much shorter threshold: ≥5 minutes of continuous seizure activity, or two or more seizures in succession without regaining consciousness in between. SE is a medical emergency requiring immediate attention. Synonyms: convulsive status epilepticus, SE.

The time threshold actually varies by seizure type: tonic-clonic seizures ≥5 minutes, focal seizures with impaired consciousness ≥10 minutes, absence seizures 10–15 minutes.

Classification
  • With prominent motor features: convulsive (tonic-clonic), myoclonic (± coma), focal motor, tonic, hyperkinetic
  • Without prominent motor features (nonconvulsive status epilepticus, NCSE): with or without coma, absence, or focal (e.g., aphasia, impaired consciousness, ongoing autonomic/sensory symptoms)
Epidemiology
  • ~60,000 cases in the US per year
  • About half occur in children
  • Two-thirds occur in individuals with no known prior seizure history
  • Of patients with a diagnosed epilepsy syndrome, ~1% will progress to SE
Etiology

Medication-related: noncompliance, a recent change, or withdrawal of antiepileptic drugs. Structural/acquired: recent cerebrovascular event, cerebral infection, head trauma, a developing neoplasm, anoxic brain injury, late-stage neurodegenerative disease. Toxic/metabolic: alcohol withdrawal, recreational drug use, drug toxicity (e.g., tricyclic antidepressants, isoniazid), electrolyte imbalance (hyponatremia, hypocalcemia), metabolic disturbances (hypoglycemia, uremia, porphyria), arteritis. Infectious: CNS infections (e.g., cerebral malaria, neurocysticercosis, viral encephalitis, prion disease).

2 Clinical Presentation
Typical course

Usually begins as a tonic-clonic seizure, but can also start as a complex partial (focal impaired-awareness) seizure. Presents as repetitive seizures, each lasting less than 2 minutes, with no return of consciousness between events — that lack of an interictal recovery period is the key feature, not just seizure duration alone.

Don't miss nonconvulsive status epilepticus

Maintain a high level of suspicion for NCSE in a patient with persistently altered mental status following a seizure, or otherwise unexplained altered mental status, bizarre behavior, autonomic dysfunction, or sensory symptoms — NCSE has no dramatic convulsive movements to flag it clinically.

3 Diagnostic Workup
CategoryFindings / Use
EEGConfirms ongoing seizure activity; essential for diagnosing NCSE, which has no reliable clinical signature otherwise
CT scanScreens for a structural cause (hemorrhage, mass, stroke)
MRIMore sensitive than CT for structural/soft-tissue causes
4 Treatment
Follow the established protocol

SE is a medical emergency requiring immediate assessment and stabilization (ABCs) — treatment follows the same phase-based acute seizure protocol built out in the Seizures & Epilepsy panel: IV benzodiazepine first-line (5–20 min), then a second-line parenteral AED (fosphenytoin, valproic acid, levetiracetam, or phenobarbital) if there's no response, then repeat second-line therapy or induce coma if still refractory. Rapidly reversible causes (hypoglycemia, electrolyte derangements, alcohol withdrawal) are treated concurrently, not sequentially.

5 Monitoring & Complications
Mortality

High overall mortality, roughly 10–50% depending on the population. More precisely, mortality is bimodal: highest in neonates (25–39%) and patients >80 years old (>50%); overall infant/child mortality ~3.6%; overall adult mortality ~15.9%.

Complications by system

Cardiac

  • Hypertension
  • Tachycardia
  • Arrhythmias

Pulmonary

  • Apnea
  • Respiratory failure
  • Hypoxia

Metabolic

  • Hyperkalemia
  • Volume depletion
  • Hyperglycemia, followed by hypoglycemia

Per the source material's LO range (1–5), this panel does not build out a separate Prevention & Health Promotion section.

Pearl

The definition that matters clinically isn't "30 minutes" — it's ≥5 minutes of continuous convulsive activity, or repeated seizures without an interictal recovery of consciousness. Waiting for the old 30-minute threshold before treating costs time the brain doesn't have.
